title: Part 6
display: Part 6 — Describing Role Structure; Reusing Content with RHEL System…

content.text: A role is a standardized directory structure that bundles everything a piece of functionality needs — tasks, handlers, default variables, templates, static files — into one self-contained, reusable, shareable unit.
main.yml holds LOW-precedence default variable values — meant to be overridden by whoever uses the role
Static files referenced by role tasks (no path needed — the role finds them automatically)
main.yml holds the role's handler definitions
main.yml holds author/license/platform/dependency info about the role itself
main.yml holds the role's actual task definitions
Jinja2 templates referenced by role tasks (same automatic path-finding as files)
An inventory + test.yml for testing the role in isolation
main.yml holds HIGH-precedence internal variables — not meant to be casually overridden

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT defaults vs. vars is a direct exam target, and it's about PRECEDENCE, not just location: defaults/main.yml variables are LOW precedence (deliberately easy to override from a playbook or inventory); vars/main.yml variables are HIGH precedence (meant for the role's internal use, resistant to being overridden). Put anything you WANT the user to customize in defaults, never vars.
Not every role needs every directory — an empty or omitted subdirectory is simply ignored.
Using a role in a playbook
For each listed role, its tasks, handlers, variables, and dependencies are pulled into the play, IN THAT ORDER. Roles listed in roles: always run BEFORE any tasks: defined directly in that same play.

⚠ WARNING Variables set inline this way (role parameters) have VERY HIGH precedence — they override nearly everything else, including inventory variables and play vars. Reusing one of these variable names elsewhere in the same play is asking for confusing, hard-to-trace bugs.
Controlling execution order: pre_tasks and post_tasks
A play's actual execution order, when everything is present, always follows this sequence:

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT Memorize this exact order — pre_tasks, then roles, then tasks, then post_tasks, with handlers firing after each stage that notified them (not just once at the very end). This is a direct, specific exam target, and it's easy to assume roles and tasks run in file order rather than this fixed sequence.

A role can also be added as an ordinary task instead of via the roles: section — include_role for dynamic (run-time) inclusion, or import_role for static (parse-time) inclusion, following the exact same static-vs-dynamic logic from Part 5's import_tasks/include_tasks.

sections.title: 2. Reusing Content with RHEL System Roles

content.text: RHEL System Roles are a set of Red Hat-provided, Red Hat-SUPPORTED roles for common subsystem configuration — included with a standard RHEL subscription, not something you write yourself.
SELinux mode, file/port contexts, booleans, SELinux users
Firewall / performance tuning (at time of writing)

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS The pitch in one sentence: RHEL 7 uses ntpd, RHEL 8 uses chronyd for time sync — managing both by hand means maintaining two different config approaches. rhel-system-roles.timesync abstracts that difference away entirely; the same role, same variables, correctly configures time sync whichever service the target host actually uses.

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT Fully Supported roles have a STABLE interface — Red Hat commits to not breaking their variables across versions. Technology Preview roles may change variables in future versions, so integration testing matters more for those. Know which tier a role is in before depending on it heavily.
Documentation for each installed role lives at /usr/share/doc/rhel-system-roles/ROLENAME/README.md, describing every variable the role accepts.
A complete example: the timesync role
One role, driven entirely by variables, correctly configures NTP on RHEL 6, 7, or 8 hosts, without the playbook author needing to know or care which underlying service each host actually uses.
Three steps, always: (1) create the role's directory structure, (2) define its content, (3) use it in a playbook.
Where Ansible looks for a role, in order
The roles/ subdirectory next to the playbook itself
Each directory in roles_path (default ~/.ansible/roles : /usr/share/ansible/roles : /etc/ansible/roles), in order
Generating the skeleton with ansible-galaxy init
This creates the complete standard directory tree automatically — faster and less error-prone than mkdir-ing each subdirectory by hand.

Task output from a role is prefixed with the role's name — a task shown as TASK [motd : deliver motd file] instantly tells you which role produced it, invaluable once a playbook uses several roles at once.

A variable defined in defaults/main.yml gets overridden, in increasing precedence, by: inventory host/group variables, then variables set inline where the role is called (role parameters, from Section 6.1) — which is exactly the same variable precedence logic from Part 2, just applied specifically to a role's low-precedence defaults.
motd_message: "Welcome to the production web tier"

Ansible Galaxy (galaxy.ansible.com) is a public hub of community-contributed roles — and the ansible-galaxy command-line tool that manages them also works against your own private Git repositories, not just the public site.

search results are alphabetical, NOT ranked by quality/popularity (the website's Best Match score is a web-only feature) — info pulls detailed metadata (license, download count, min_ansible_version) from the role's meta/main.yml and its GitHub repo.
Without -p, roles install into the first writable directory in roles_path — normally ~/.ansible/roles.
Installing a project's full role set with requirements.yml
A roles/requirements.yml file acts as a dependency manifest, letting a whole set of roles be installed in one command instead of one-by-one — and it isn't limited to Ansible Galaxy itself:
# from Ansible Galaxy, specific version, renamed locally
# from a Git repository over HTTPS
The Galaxy role name, OR a URL if not hosted on Galaxy
git or hg — required only for source-control-hosted roles; omitted for Galaxy/tarball sources
A branch, tag, or commit hash to pin
Overrides the local directory name the role is installed as

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT A requirements.yml is the standard way real projects pin exact role versions for reproducibility — installing 'whatever the latest role happens to be today' is a real source of playbooks breaking unexpectedly months later. Pin versions the same way you'd pin package versions in any other dependency file.

labs.title: Lab: Build, Use, and Reuse a Role

content.text: Create a custom role from scratch, use it alongside a RHEL System Role in one play with correct execution ordering, and pin a Galaxy role via requirements.yml.
New servers need: a standard MOTD banner (your own role), correct time synchronization (a RHEL System Role), and a verification step that runs before anything else to confirm connectivity.
A control node with a project directory ~/ansible-lab6, an inventory group [newservers]
1. Run ansible-galaxy init to scaffold a role named motd_banner
2. Fill in tasks/main.yml (a template task deploying a banner to /etc/motd) and defaults/main.yml (a default banner message variable)

3. Write a playbook targeting newservers with: a pre_tasks ping check, roles: listing both motd_banner and rhel-system-roles.timesync (with timesync_ntp_servers set), and confirm the motd_banner role's default message can be overridden inline
4. Create roles/requirements.yml pinning one real Galaxy role (e.g. geerlingguy.redis) at a specific version, and install it with ansible-galaxy

Remember the fixed order from Section 6.1: pre_tasks run first, then everything in roles: (in the order listed), then tasks:. Your ping check belongs in pre_tasks specifically so it runs before either role does anything.

Before checking the solution: does overriding motd_banner's message inline in the roles: section actually take effect? If not, double check the variable is defined in defaults/main.yml (low precedence, overridable) and not accidentally in vars/main.yml (high precedence, resistant to override).
motd_message: "This system is managed by Ansible."
ansible-galaxy init generates the full standard skeleton in one command, avoiding manual mkdir/touch of eight subdirectories.
motd_message lives in defaults/main.yml specifically so it's LOW precedence and cleanly overridable — exactly per Section 6.1's precedence rule.
pre_tasks: guarantees the ping check runs before either role, matching the fixed pre_tasks → roles → tasks → post_tasks order from Section 6.1.
requirements.yml pins geerlingguy.redis at an exact version — reproducible across every machine that later runs ansible-galaxy install -r on this same file.

cat /etc/motd on a managed host should show the default banner text; overriding motd_message inline in roles: (motd_banner then a nested vars: or inline var) should change that output on the next run. ansible-galaxy list should show geerlingguy.redis at exactly version 1.6.0.

This lab's shape — a small custom role for something org-specific (a banner), a Red Hat-supported System Role for something standard (time sync), and a pinned third-party role for something common (Redis) — is genuinely how mature Ansible projects are composed: write only what's actually unique to you, reuse everything else.
Q1. What's the precedence difference between a role's defaults/main.yml and vars/main.yml variables?

Answer: defaults/main.yml is LOW precedence, meant to be easily overridden by whoever uses the role; vars/main.yml is HIGH precedence, meant for the role's own internal use and resistant to casual override.
Q2. When a play has pre_tasks, roles, tasks, and post_tasks all defined, what's the execution order?
Answer: pre_tasks → roles → tasks → post_tasks, with any notified handlers firing after each stage that notified them.
Q3. Do roles listed in roles: run before or after that play's own tasks: list?
Answer: Before — roles always run first, ahead of any tasks defined directly in the play.
Q4. What's the practical benefit of rhel-system-roles.timesync over writing your own time-sync tasks?
Answer: It abstracts away the difference between chronyd (RHEL 7/8) and ntpd (RHEL 6) — one role, one set of variables, correctly configures either underlying service.
Q5. What's the practical difference between a Fully Supported and a Technology Preview RHEL System Role?

Answer: Fully Supported roles have a stable interface Red Hat commits to keeping unchanged; Technology Preview roles may change their variables in future versions, so integration testing matters more.
Q6. What command generates a new role's complete standard directory structure automatically?
Q7. In what order does Ansible search for a role by default?
Answer: First the roles/ subdirectory next to the playbook, then each directory listed in roles_path in order (default: ~/.ansible/roles, /usr/share/ansible/roles, /etc/ansible/roles).
Q8. What does a requirements.yml file let you do that ansible-galaxy install alone doesn't as conveniently?
Answer: Install and pin a whole SET of roles (from Galaxy, Git repos, or tarballs, each at a specific version) in one command, instead of installing and version-pinning each role individually.
Q9. What precedence level do variables set INLINE where a role is called (role parameters) have?
Answer: Very high — they override nearly everything else, including inventory variables and play vars, which is why reusing those variable names elsewhere in the same play is risky.
Q10. What's the difference between include_role and import_role?

Answer: The same static-vs-dynamic distinction as Part 5's include_tasks/import_tasks — include_role is resolved dynamically at run time, import_role is resolved statically when the playbook is parsed.
RH294 — RED HAT SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION III: LINUX AUTOMATION

This Part covers RH294 Chapter 9 in full: diagnosing broken playbooks before they run, reading and controlling execution output, safely testing changes with check mode, and tracking down the connection/privilege problems that account for most real managed-host failures.

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS Every other RH294 Part has been about writing automation. This one is about what happens the moment it doesn't work — which, in real infrastructure work, is often more of the job than the writing itself.
